text:
"𝙅𝙪𝙣𝙞𝙤𝙧𝙨 𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙙𝙞𝙨𝙖𝙥𝙥𝙚𝙖𝙧𝙞𝙣𝙜. 𝙏𝙝𝙚𝙧𝙚'𝙨 𝙣𝙤 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙩𝙝𝙚𝙢 𝙖𝙣𝙮𝙢𝙤𝙧𝙚."

I keep hearing this. And honestly? 𝗜'𝗺 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱.

Here's what I’m actually observing: 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻.
A year ago, a junior needed to learn React. 
Now, a junior needs to learn Claude Code. 
𝘛𝘩𝘢𝘵'𝘴 𝘪𝘵. That's the whole revolution.


𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆? 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗲𝘀.
When the internal combustion engine appeared, tractors replaced horses in the fields. There was a transition period, sure. 

But here's what happened: young people who quickly learned to work with tractors — they came in and displaced the farmers who insisted on doing everything with horses because they "didn't want to use the new thing."

Same story. Different century.

__________________________________________


And the other thing is 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁.

Yes, AI writes code faster. 
But if you take a task end-to-end, it doesn't get done 5x faster. It gets done maybe 30% faster.

So the market "shrank" by 30%. But the amount of work? 
According to my research, it grew by 50%. Maybe 100%. 
Because AI has created entirely new business niches. 
New products, new ideas, new automation needs — way more than existed a year or two ago.

__________________________________________


Will there be a transition period? Sure. 
Maybe six months. Maybe a year.
But 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴.
There will be more of it. It's just going to look different. 
𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗽𝘁 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁? 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆'𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲.

Actually, they'll be better than fine.

The paper synthesizes personal theoretical research and data analysis (including the GitKraken 2025, DORA, and McKinsey reports) to demonstrate that AI adoption is not uniform, but generates three distinct cognitive classes:
L1 (Passengers): Dependent users, characterized by cognitive atrophy and the "uncertainty-reassurance cycle".
L2 (Operators): Clerks who maintain existing systems but are at maximum risk from automation.
L3 (Architects): A small elite that enters into symbiosis with AI (Homo Symbioticus), achieving exponential productivity gains.
